passages.happening:
‘When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel’ (verse 1), they come to Zerubbabel and the heads of the families with an offer. “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here” (verse 2).

Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the other heads of families refuse: “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us” (verse 3).

Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build. ‘They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with a sound heard from afar. Chapter 4 shows who heard it.

The people who come with the offer say that they were brought to the land by Esarhaddon, king of Assyria from 681 to 669 BC. Assyria had deported the people of the northern kingdom after Samaria fell in 722 BC and settled people from other lands in their place. This verse suggests that more were settled under Esarhaddon. These groups, in and around Samaria, are among the ancestors of the people later known as Samaritans, though the full break between Jews and Samaritans came later.

Building a temple in the ancient world was a political act as well as a religious one. A temple gave a community a center, a treasury and a claim on the land. To share the work would have meant sharing the identity of the community itself. The returnees also make a legal point: Cyrus's permission had been given to them.

Their neighbors, for their part, had lived on the land for generations. They may well have seen the returnees as newcomers claiming authority over a region that was not theirs. The book calls them ‘the enemies of Judah and Benjamin’ (verse 1), and what they do next, from discouragement to hired counselors, shows why.
passages.later:
Second Kings describes the peoples the Assyrians settled in the north: ‘They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away’ (2 Kings 17:33).

Centuries later the rift was deep. When a Samaritan woman meets Jesus at a well, John adds a note for his readers: ‘For Jews do not associate with Samaritans’ (John 4:9).
passages.hard:
Were Zerubbabel and Jeshua right to refuse the help of people who said they worshiped the same God?

The refusal can look narrow to a modern reader. The people who offered help said they sought the same God and had sacrificed to him for generations, and their later hostility could be read as a reaction to being turned away. On the other hand, Second Kings describes these settlers as worshiping the LORD while serving their own gods, and the book presents the offer as coming from adversaries whose later actions show their intent. The returnees' concern was not the purity of a bloodline as such but the integrity of worship. A temple shared with a mixed religion would no longer be the house of the LORD alone.

Interpreters differ in emphasis. Some read the chapter as a necessary act of faithfulness at a fragile moment, when the small community could easily have been absorbed. Others note that the prophets of the period, and later the New Testament, looked for a day when the nations would join in the worship of the LORD, and they see the chapter as one stage in God's purposes rather than a permanent rule. Most agree that the text itself approves the refusal, and grounds it in Cyrus's decree and in the worship of the LORD alone.

Either way, the chapter gives no one a reason to look down on any people, then or now.
passages.asks: The offer sounded generous, and it came with a cost the builders would not pay. Ask where you have been offered help that would have changed what you are. And ask how you can hold firmly to what matters most without treating others with contempt.

passages.t: Accusations, and a letter to the king
passages.happening:
‘At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem’ (verse 6). Under King Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their associates write to him, and the chapter notes, ‘It was written in Aramaic and then translated’ (verse 7).

Then comes the letter itself. Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe write ‘the letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes’ (verse 8), on behalf of officials and peoples settled in Samaria and elsewhere west of the Euphrates. They tell the king that the Jews who came from him have returned to Jerusalem, ‘And they are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city, restoring its walls, and repairing its foundations’ (verse 12).

If the city is rebuilt, they warn, ‘they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer’ (verse 13). They urge the king to search the records of his fathers, where he will find that the city is ‘a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, inciting sedition from ancient times’ (verse 15). If its walls are restored, ‘you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
These verses jump forward in time. Verse 5 has already reached Darius I, who reigned from 522 to 486 BC. Verse 6 moves on to Xerxes (486 to 465 BC), and verses 7 to 23 to Artaxerxes I (465 to 424 BC). The letter is not about the temple, which was finished in 515 BC, but about the city's walls.

At verse 8 the book itself changes language, from Hebrew to Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, and it stays in Aramaic until 6:18. Verse 7 even says the letter was written in Aramaic.

The Persian empire ran on written reports and royal archives, and these verses show the system at work. The letters follow the standard official form: who is writing, to whom, a greeting, and phrases such as ‘Let it be known to the king’ (verse 12). The writers name the peoples settled in Samaria by the great Ashurbanipal, the Assyrian king who reigned from about 669 to 631 BC (verse 10).

Their argument is shrewd. They say nothing about religion. They appeal to the king's revenue and the king's security. And their charge has truth in it. Judah had rebelled against both Assyria and Babylon, and its enemies use its real history against it.

The word for accusation in verse 6, sitnah, comes from the same root as satan, which means adversary or accuser. The opposition works through legal complaint.
passages.later:
Jerusalem's kings had indeed rebelled. Of Hezekiah, Second Kings says, ‘He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him’ (2 Kings 18:7). Of the last king, ‘Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon’ (2 Kings 24:20).

The king named in verse 6 is the Xerxes of the book of Esther, ‘who reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush’ (Esther 1:1).
passages.hard:
Why does the chapter jump from Darius to Xerxes and Artaxerxes, and then come back to Darius?

The writer steps outside the order of time to gather several episodes of opposition, spanning about ninety years, into one account. Verse 5 mentions Darius, verses 6 to 23 look ahead to later kings, and verse 24 returns to the reign of Darius, where chapter 5 picks up the story. The repeated mention of Darius in verses 5 and 24 frames the leap forward, a technique ancient writers used to show a pattern.

The effect is to show that the opposition was not a passing setback. It was the ongoing condition of the returned community, under one king after another. A reader who takes the chapter as a strict sequence will be confused; a reader who sees the pattern will see what the book means.
passages.asks: The accusers used Judah's real past against it. Ask how you answer when your own history is used against you. And ask whether you have ever used someone else's past to stop them from building something good.

passages.t: The king's reply, and the work stops
passages.happening:
The king writes back to Rehum, Shimshai and their associates ‘living in Samaria and elsewhere in the region west of the Euphrates’ (verse 17). The letter has been read in his presence. He ordered a search, and ‘It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition’ (verse 19). Mighty kings once ruled over Jerusalem and received tribute from the whole region.

So the order goes out: ‘issue an order for these men to stop, so that this city will not be rebuilt until I so order’ (verse 21). As soon as the letter is read to them, Rehum and Shimshai go to the Jews in Jerusalem ‘and forcibly stopped them’ (verse 23).

The chapter ends by coming back to the temple: ‘Thus the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The king has the archives searched, as the accusers asked, and the archives confirm their charge. Jerusalem had rebelled against Assyria and Babylon. The machinery of empire turns against God's people here. But the same archives will be searched again in chapters 5 and 6, and that time they will restart the work.

Notice the king's words, ‘until I so order’ (verse 21). The stop is not forever. The same King Artaxerxes would later send Nehemiah to Jerusalem with letters for timber to rebuild its gates and walls. This order is probably the background to the broken walls Nehemiah hears about in 445 BC.

In Aramaic, the verb to stop or cease comes four times at the chapter's end. The king orders the builders to stop, they are stopped by force, and the work ceases. The repetition makes the stoppage feel heavy and final, which sets up the surprise of chapter 5.

Verse 24 returns to the temple and the reign of Darius. The temple work had stood still since the early years, and it would not move again until 520 BC.
passages.later: When news of Jerusalem reached Nehemiah at the Persian court, it was this: ‘The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire’ (Nehemiah 1:3). And the second year of Darius, when the work began again, is the year of Haggai's first message: ‘In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet’ (Haggai 1:1).
passages.asks: The work stopped, by force, for years. Ask how you respond when faithful work is stopped by people with power over it. And ask what it would mean to wait, as these builders did, without letting go of what God had given them to do.
